talks.title: Classical OSINT using AI Actual Intelligence
talks.teaser: Presents the ACTUAL framework for turning open-source findings into validated intelligence, using a fictional missing-person case to show how to weigh sources and state confidence.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that investigators now have more tools, automation and AI than ever, yet still make familiar errors: accepting the first result, trusting repeated content, and mistaking collected information for intelligence. The speaker argues that when tools are unavailable or wrong, analytical method is what remains, and introduces a framework called ACTUAL. Each letter maps to a step: asking well-defined questions, moving toward primary sources, testing assumptions, weighing context, and linking evidence so every conclusion can be justified with a stated level of confidence.

To show the method in practice, the speaker works through a fictional missing-person case built only from public material. The clues include a library exit time, a bus schedule that had already stopped running, a campus parking structure, a family cabin mentioned in an old newspaper article, mobile coverage maps, and two conflicting sightings. Each clue is checked against the others, weak leads are downgraded, and competing explanations are compared. The route and timing favour a voluntary trip over foul play, but the speaker stresses that a lack of evidence for harm is not proof of safety.

The takeaway is that tools gather material, but the investigator decides what matters. Practitioners should write down their assumptions, look for evidence that would disprove a working theory, and express findings as low, moderate or high confidence rather than certainty.

talks.title: What it takes to find missing people
talks.teaser: Explores how gamified OSINT contests help locate missing people, covering the roles of participant, coach and report writer, plus practical search tactics.
talks.summary:
A Trace Labs panel looked at how gamified open-source intelligence is used to find missing people. The moderator, a Trace Labs director, was joined by a participant who had won the top individual prize, a long-time coach, and the team lead for reporting. They described the workflow: participants search during timed capture-the-flag events, coaches review submissions and award points, and the reporting team later packages the findings for law enforcement, with the goal of giving families answers.

Much of the discussion focused on method. Each discovered detail should be treated as a pivot toward the next lead. Teams benefit from clear notes and from agreeing on skills early, since a member without social media can still contribute through documentation or public records. Panelists warned about the wrong-person trap: when investigators fixate on a candidate, they should actively try to disprove the match. Narrowing search dates to the period before someone vanished can cut through news noise, and relatives named on missing-person posters often lead to new material.

The speakers also stressed the human side. The work can surface disturbing material, so participants should know when to step back and talk to their team. They noted that many people keep a public account and a private one. Their advice for newcomers was to start with search engines and free online videos, examine your own digital footprint first, and learn by doing. A single verified fact can be the missing piece that investigators need.
